newsitem.title: INDONESIA: More pain seen for Indonesian markets this week.
newsitem.headline: More pain seen for Indonesian markets this week.

text.p: Indonesian financial markets are likely to slip again this week despite President Suharto's efforts to quell panic selling of stocks and the rupiah currency, analysts said on Sunday.

They said the president's annual state-of-the-nation address on Saturday, in which he promised to cut back spending and maintain tight monetary and fiscal policies, would only provide temporary relief, if any, to the beleagured rupiah.
The unit was floated last week after the central bank decided that defending it in the wake of sustained pressure on all regional currencies would be prohibitively expensive.
The rupiah then fell sharply and closed in Jakarta at an historic low of 2,900 against the dollar on Friday.
The currency has lost more than 20 percent of its value so far this year. Dealers said the market was losing confidence in it, and some said sentiment could get worse this week.

"We may indeed go to the 3,000 level before the rupiah begins to recover towards more sustainable levels in line with its basic fundamentals, when we would see the rupiah somewhere between 2,600 and 2,700 to the dollar," Bill Belchere, head of Asian fixed income research at Merrill Lynch, said on Friday.
Things were no better on the stock market, and traders said they expected the index to fall below 600 points.
It closed at 617.71 points on Friday, the lowest level this year, after falling more than 100 points since the beginning of the month on the rupiah weakness.
"Everyone is looking to when Thailand will remove its two-tier (currency) system," said Jimmy Koh, regional economist at the I.D.E.A. consultancy in Singapore.
"If that happens, there will be a scramble for dollars and the baht could fall," he said. "That will have another spillover effect on the rupiah."

Some analysts have said Thailand's two-tier currency market -- one offshore and the other onshore -- could be ended this week, but others have said the move may be postponed until some investor confidence returns to the battered economy.
Koh said Suharto's speech was positive on the economy but any effect on the currency market would be limited.
"It all depends on how the dollar fares against the regionals. You can't view the rupiah in isolation, it has to be seen as one of a group of (Southeast Asian) currencies."

Analysts have also said that unhedged corporate borrowings are worrisome. They estimate that some 10 percent of Indonesian corporate borrowings of about $58 billion are unhedged, and say they have noticed a scramble to cover positions, further weakening the rupiah.
Kian Guntur, a trader at PT Schroders Indonesia, said stock market activity would be slow on Monday because of a holiday in Hong Kong.
But he forecast the market was headed below 600 points.
"Any prop-up will be an opportunity for people to sell more," he said.
Other dealers said small investors were buying dollars and gold in the wake of the rupiah's weakness, while domestic mutual funds were being hit by a slew of redemptions.
They said some funds were being pressured by the government to support the market, but would have little opportunity to do so in the current environment.

High interest rates because of the tight monetary and fiscal policies, the likelihood of a prolonged drought and a sharp fall in the Dow Jones industrial average on Friday were also bearish factors, they said.
But analysts said the current speculation-driven woes did not reflect any fundamental weakness in the economy and that the fall in the rupiah did have some silver linings.
They said exports would be more competitive and that growth in non-oil exports would put the economy on an even more sound footing.
"Indonesia is not like Thailand in any way. However, it's a very nervous market, said Belchere of Merrill Lynch.
"You cannot contain the effect of spillover in the medium-term. However, in the longer-term we are sure Indonesia has very fine economic prospects."
